title: Making a Shaker peg rail
subtitle: Make and fit a traditional Shaker-style peg rail from a length of hardwood or softwood with turned or square pegs
excerpt: How to make a traditional Shaker peg rail with a shaped backboard and dowel pegs. Covers cutting and shaping the backboard, drilling the peg holes, gluing the pegs, finishing the wood, and fixing to the wall.
sourceNotes: Traditional Shaker furniture-making practice, documented in US public domain sources (pre-1928). Period furniture pattern books.

glossaryTerms.definition: A wall-mounted strip of wood with evenly spaced dowel pegs, a characteristic feature of Shaker domestic interiors. The Shakers used peg rails in every room for hanging chairs, tools, garments, and household objects to keep floors clear. Typical dimensions: 90 to 120 mm wide backboard, pegs at 200 to 250 mm centres, peg length 100 to 120 mm.

content.text: is a simple workshop project: a shaped backboard with regularly spaced dowel pegs. The work is cutting and shaping the backboard, drilling peg holes at a consistent angle, gluing in the dowels, and applying a finish. It makes for a compact, practical wall fitting.

Cut the backboard from 90 x 19 mm planed softwood (PAR) or hardwood to the required length. The classic Shaker profile has a shallow step or chamfer along the bottom edge of the backboard. Mark the peg centres at 200 to 250 mm intervals along the centre line of the backboard. Mark the fixing screw positions (at each end and every 600 mm) on the same centre line.

Fit a 19 mm or 25 mm flat bit or Forstner bit to the drill. Drill each peg hole at a slight upward angle of about 5 to 10 degrees so the peg tilts upward in use and items hung on it slide toward the wall rather than off the end. Drill to a depth that matches the length of the peg tenon (typically 25 to 30 mm). Keep the angle consistent across all holes; a simple angled guide block clamped to the backboard helps.

Sand all faces of the backboard smooth through 120, 180, and 240 grit. Ease all arrises (sharp edges) lightly with the sanding block. Apply paint, oil, wax, or a light stain to all faces before fitting the pegs, as the areas immediately around the peg holes are difficult to finish once the pegs are in.

Buy or turn Shaker-style wooden pegs with a short tenon that fits the drilled hole. Apply a small amount of wood glue (PVA) to each tenon, push firmly into the hole at the correct upward angle, and twist slightly to spread the glue. Wipe away excess glue immediately. Allow the glue to cure for 24 hours before loading the pegs.
Fix the rail to the wall

Mark the fixing screw positions on the wall using the spirit level to ensure the rail is perfectly horizontal. Drill and plug the wall, then screw through the backboard into the wall plugs. Cover the screw heads with wooden cover buttons (mushroom-headed plugs) that press into a slightly larger shallow recess counterbored over the screw hole.

attrs.cause: Peg holes drilled horizontally rather than with an upward angle, or pegs glued with the angle pointing downward.
attrs.fix: On the next rail, drill the holes with a consistent 5 to 10-degree upward angle. Drooping pegs on an existing rail can be reinforced with a small wooden wedge driven alongside the peg tenon.

attrs.cause: Peg tenon too short or glue not applied.
attrs.fix: A minimum 25 mm tenon depth is required. Re-drill the hole to the correct depth, cut a new peg, and re-glue.
